items.summary: Finite-time binding measurements constrain kinetic rates through both a reaction model and its calibration parameters. We characterize the sharp upper bound for the association rate in a three-state conformational-selection model when the dissociation rate, conformational rate, equilibrium constant and concentration scale belong to a prescribed compact joint set. The observations are calibrated bound fractions subject to finitely many closed interval constraints. We first prove that each finite-time bound fraction is strictly increasing in the initial binding-competent population. The physical feasible set at a fixed calibration is therefore an interval in that population. Let V be the calibration parameters with a nonempty physical feasible interval and let C = cl(V) within the joint calibration set. The sharp rate supremum is the reciprocal of the minimum of lambda K0 L / b on C, where L is the lower inverse threshold. Uniform finiteness is equivalent to a positive joint separation from the zero-population limiting curve on C. Explicit examples distinguish pointwise finiteness from uniform finiteness, inaccessible closed boundary points from physical limiting models, and separation by different readings from separation by one fixed reading. A continuous calibration example admits a certified sharp bound. We also state the optical conditions needed to interpret fluorescence as bound population.
items.title: Sharp Identification Bounds for Binding Rates under Joint Calibration Uncertainty

items.summary: This record contains version 11 of the replication materials for “When a Digital Audit Trail Becomes Audit Evidence: Source Selection and Identification under Ambiguous Reconciliation,” accompanying the manuscript and proposed online appendix. items.summary: Code, data, results and figures for the manuscript "Parameter Identifiability Limits in Dynamic Modelling and Control of a Brackish-Water Reverse Osmosis System" (A.G. Gadallah, submitted). A lumped nonlinear solution-diffusion model of a brackish-water RO pilot plant (Ansari et al., Clean. Eng. Technol. 4 (2021) 100134) is identified from a 5 x 5 operating grid reconstructed from the published regressions, validated on two withheld salinity levels and used unchanged for control analysis. The analysis shows that the salt permeability is practically non-identifiable from permeate-flow data and traces the consequences into permeate-quality prediction, the stability margins of the quality loop, the stability of optimised tunings and the comparison of decentralised PI and one-way feedforward control, including the role of valve and conductivity-sensor dynamics. King Saud Univ. Eng. Sci. 36 (2024) 438-445); all results (CSV, JSON, Data.xlsx) and figures. items.summary: This deposit contains the model code, the complete parameter set with provenance labels, all numerical outputs, and the scripts required to regenerate every figure and table in the associated manuscript. The work is a physiologically based kinetic (PBK) analysis of the renal exposure window of emodin, an anthraquinone of rhubarb. The model is an eight-compartment, perfusion-limited PBK model with intestinal and hepatic first-pass metabolism, biliary excretion and enterohepatic recirculation, parameterised for mouse, rat and human. No experimental data were generated: the study is entirely computational. items.summary: This repository contains supporting materials for the revision of Frontiers in Digital Health manuscript 1986016, examining prior-window home bioimpedance variability and subsequent affected-to-unaffected arm ECW/TBW ratio excursions. The package includes aggregate statistical outputs from the revised analyses, portable Python analysis scripts, a fully synthetic example dataset, variable definitions, analysis provenance, and validation documentation. The supporting materials cover within- and between-participant analyses, observation-weight diagnostics, nonlinear analyses, calendar-time sensitivity analyses, and model convergence assessments. Version 3 update: This version adds materials prepared in response to the subsequent minor-revision review. The new materials include the corrected unaffected-arm comparator using working-independence logistic generalized estimating equations with participant-cluster robust sandwich covariance, the exact-timestamp deduplication and acquisition-time ordering audit, and additional numerical-stability and convergence documentation. Actual participant-level longitudinal measurements, clinical records, identifiers, and ultrasound images are not included because of privacy and ethical restrictions. The synthetic dataset demonstrates the analysis workflow; it does not represent study participants or reproduce the observed study estimates. Exact recomputation of the observed analyses requires authorized access to the restricted source data. These materials supplement the parent-study materials available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22934011 . The manuscript is currently under revision and has not been accepted or published.
items.title: Revision analysis code, aggregate results and synthetic example for prior-window home bioimpedance variability and subsequent interlimb ratio excursions

items.summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-five entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, and carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters.
items.title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

items.summary: Runtime query similarity identification supports several activities, including workload analysis, identifying recurring behaviour, auditing, debugging, and anomaly detection. Existing methods for evaluating query similarity mostly rely on SQL text, execution plans, or result values but do not account for input data or how results are derived during query execution. This paper proposes a novel approach using data provenance for query-template identification. We construct query-level profiles that capture explicit data dependencies, occurrence frequencies, and structural properties by aggregating tuple-level Lineage and Why-provenance across entire query results. We also derive Provenance Structural Descriptors (PSD), which summarise these profiles using a small set of numerical features. We evaluate our proposals using these profiles to identify query templates over \(12{,}500\) distinct query instances generated from parametrised TPC-DS query templates. The experimental evaluation shows that query templates can be identified solely from their provenance footprints, and that accuracy improves as more historical data becomes available. It also shows that PSD achieve high classification accuracy with limited training history and low test-processing cost.
items.title: Data Provenance Aggregation and Structural Descriptors for Query-Template Identification

items.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly deployed through black-box APIs and trained on large collections of real-world tabular datasets. As this training paradigm becomes more widely adopted, private or proprietary datasets may be incorporated into pre-training corpora, yet there are currently no dedicated methods for determining whether a given tabular dataset was used to train a TFM. As a solution, we introduce the first dataset inference method for TFMs, aiming to infer whether a suspect dataset was part of a model's pre-training data. We systematically analyze a broad collection of candidate signals that can be observed from a black-box TFM via input manipulation and find that individual signals provide only weak evidence of training data membership. However, by combining multiple complementary signals, we can infer dataset membership for several state-of-the-art TFMs trained on real tabular data, achieving up to 0.99 ROCAUC dependent on the TFM. We then study factors that influence dataset identification, including pre-training data composition, model capacity, and the use of real vs. synthetic data. Our results show that our dataset inference method is a practical auditing tool for detecting privacy leakage and the use of proprietary datasets in TFMs.
items.title: Dataset Inference for Data Provenance and Privacy Auditing in Tabular Foundation Models

items.summary: This repository contains the complete 10-water-year daily streamflow simulation archive ( 1989-10-01 through 1999-09-30 ; 3,652 daily steps across 531 canonical CAMELS-US basins) for ERA-Multi-Paradigm-Gauged (10-model ensemble) , evaluated as part of the CAMELS-US Hydrological Model Intercomparison Project (MIP) ( grey-nearing/camels-us-mip ). Model Name: ERA-Multi-Paradigm-Gauged (10-model ensemble) Target Leaderboard: gauged__multi_camels Spatial Evaluation Regime: Gauged Basins (All 531 Basins Trained & Evaluated) Meteorological Forcings: Multi-Forcing (Daymet + Maurer + NLDAS) Ensemble Size: n = 10 independent random seed realizations ( seeds = 100..109 ) Open-Source Model Code: https://github.com/grey-nearing/camels-us-mip/tree/main/models/era_gauged_multi_paradigm ERA Discovery Notebook: https://github.com/grey-nearing/camels-us-mip/blob/main/era_experiments/era_gauged_newman_cv_winner.ipynb Model Architecture & Experimental Protocol Architecture: Four-Family Multi-Paradigm Hydrological Ensemble combining two complementary feature-and-conditioning paradigms per seed: (1) Paradigm A (60 multi-scale hydroclimatic, PET, rolling water-balance deficit, and cross-forcing agreement features with basin-conditioned static embeddings, trajectory Huber-NSE + log1p MSE loss, and exponential moving average weight averaging): `CausalConvGRULSTM` (multi-scale causal dilated Conv1D d=1,3,9 + coupled GRU-LSTM, weight 0.38) and `MultiScaleFiLMEALSTM` (2-layer FiLM-modulated Entity-Aware LSTM, weight 0.12); and (2) Paradigm B (36 clean meteorological features augmented with continuous 10-year 3-forcing degree-day snowpack accumulation/melt and liquid water delivery across Daymet, Maurer, and NLDAS, conditioned strictly on 27 static catchment attributes with zero basin ID lookup embeddings): `DualPathwayFiLMGRULSTM` (parallel 2-layer LSTM + 2-layer GRU with static FiLM gates, weight 0.36) and `EntityAwareHydroLSTM` (2-layer Entity-Aware HydroLSTM, weight 0.14), evaluated with hybrid continuous 10-year rollout + overlapping 730-day sliding-window inference. Strict Non-Leakage Protocol: Architecture and blending weights discovered strictly within the Newman et al. (2015) training decade (`1998-10-01` to `2008-09-30`, XID 304144117, achieving `0.8410` Median NSE on the `1999-10-01` to `2003-09-30` validation split when trained on `2003-10-01` to `2008-09-30`), with zero access to the `1989-10-01` to `1999-09-30` Newman evaluation period. For benchmark evaluation, 10 independent random seeds (`seeds = 100..109`) of all 4 architectural families (40 trained models total) were trained on the full Newman training window (`1999-10-01` to `2008-09-30`, with 365-day spinup `1998-10-01` to `1999-09-30`) and evaluated out-of-sample on the blind Newman test period (`1989-10-01` to `1999-09-30`; 3,652 days across 531 basins). Benchmark Performance Summary (531 CAMELS-US Basins, 1989-10-01 to 1999-09-30) Ensemble Median NSE (n = 10): 0.826 Single-Model Median NSE (mean ± SD across 10 seeds): 0.822 ± 0.002 Ensemble Mean NSE: 0.776 Ensemble Median KGE: 0.806 Ensemble Median Peak-Flow Bias |FHV|: 13.28% Catastrophic Failure Basins (NSE ≤ 0): 2 / 531 Included Files era_gauged_multi_paradigm_gauged_multi_camels_hydrographs_531x3652.npz : Compressed NumPy archive containing qsim / qsim_members of shape (10, 531, 3652) (float32, mm/day), qsim_ensemble_mean of shape (531, 3652) , qobs of shape (531, 3652) , basins of shape (531,) , dates of shape (3652,) , and seeds of shape (10,) . era_gauged_multi_paradigm_gauged_multi_camels.zarr.zip : Consolidated Zarr v2 store containing qsim (531, 3652) , qsim_members (10, 531, 3652) , basin (531,) , date (3652,) , huc_02 (531,) , and member (10,) . README.md : Complete documentation, schema reference, and Python loading example.
items.title: CAMELS-US Hydrological Model Intercomparison Project (MIP) — ERA-Multi-Paradigm-Gauged (10-model ensemble) Daily Streamflow Hydrographs (531 Basins, Water Years 1990–1999)

The experimental evaluation shows that query templates can be identified solely from their provenance footprints, and that accuracy improves as more historical data becomes available. It also shows that PSD achieve high classification accuracy with limited training history and low test-processing cost.
items.title: Data Provenance Aggregation and Structural Descriptors for Query-Template Identification

items.summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-five entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, and carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters.
items.title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

items.summary: This record contains version 11 of the replication materials for “When a Digital Audit Trail Becomes Audit Evidence: Source Selection and Identification under Ambiguous Reconciliation,” accompanying the manuscript and proposed online appendix. The deposited file is 187_Replication_Materials_v11.zip. The archive supplies data, code, source-linked results and finite checks while distinguishing historical evidence from constructed mathematical examples. It includes source-conditioned reconciliation cases and finite query design; the one-query identification characterization and bounded-answer-error checks; source-bundled certificates, exact fault-budget thresholds and witness checks; named-absence query games, the fraction-of-deficit expected-cost derivation and randomized switching checks; and the bounded-unavailability proof, reconstruction comparison and finite validations. The expected-query-cost result assumes complete local candidate graphs, exact always-available unit-cost pair answers, free computation, and zero-error worst-input expected cost; it does not extend to arbitrary source-constrained graphs. The unavailability result gives a sharp feasibility boundary, not an optimal positive-unavailability query rate. Historical materials include the 254-report classifier panel, generated known-truth benchmark results, corrected record-read bookkeeping for 72,000 rows, and restricted-matching and complete-log-union checks. The 85.91 percent and 92.91 percent results describe different procedures and must not be interchanged. Original-source assessments of 57 historically clean-labelled reports identify 18 explicit exceptions, five assurance uncertainties and 34 without a comparable current-year adverse qualification located. These assessments do not validate or relabel the entire panel. The classifier is not validated as a prevalence measure, and historical visibility labels are assigned model conditions rather than field outcomes. Reproduction: extract the ZIP and use Python 3.11 or newer. The portable finite-check runner requires NumPy and SciPy. Run python run_checks.py --out-dir /absolute/path/to/new-results, choosing a new output directory outside the extracted package. The runner checks MANIFEST.json, preserves inputs and writes per-script logs and CHECK_RESULTS.json. Wider frozen analyses and figure generation can also require pandas, matplotlib, pypdf, python-docx and lxml; see the README and supplied requirements. Finite replay corroborates implementations but does not replace proofs, re-extract copyrighted reports or estimate field detection performance. Rights and access: derived public-source data, documentation and generated benchmark outputs are licensed under CC BY 4.0; original code is licensed under MIT. Copyrighted papers and annual-report PDFs and licensed WRDS, Compustat, Audit Analytics and CRSP rows are excluded and are not sublicensed. Source URLs, identifiers, page references and hashes support permitted reacquisition subject to the original access conditions. No participants were recruited and no new human-subject data were collected. Funding: none. Financial conflicts of interest: none. Nonfinancial conflicts of interest: none. items.summary: Code, data, results and figures for the manuscript "Parameter Identifiability Limits in Dynamic Modelling and Control of a Brackish-Water Reverse Osmosis System" (A.G. Gadallah, submitted). A lumped nonlinear solution-diffusion model of a brackish-water RO pilot plant (Ansari et al., Clean. Eng. Technol. 4 (2021) 100134) is identified from a 5 x 5 operating grid reconstructed from the published regressions, validated on two withheld salinity levels and used unchanged for control analysis. The analysis shows that the salt permeability is practically non-identifiable from permeate-flow data and traces the consequences into permeate-quality prediction, the stability margins of the quality loop, the stability of optimised tunings and the comparison of decentralised PI and one-way feedforward control, including the role of valve and conductivity-sensor dynamics. Contents: romodel (Python model package); analysis scripts a1-a4 (identification, control analysis, common-objective re-optimisation, uncertainty propagation with Sobol indices and Monte Carlo); derive.py (collects every number quoted in the manuscript into a traceability table); make_figures.py; selftest.py; source data (reconstructed operating grid; secondary data transcribed from Sadek et al., J. King Saud Univ. Eng. Sci. 36 (2024) 438-445); all results (CSV, JSON, Data.xlsx) and figures. To reproduce: cd code; pip install -r requirements.txt; python selftest.py (1-2 min) or python run_all.py (about 70 min). Requires Python 3.10 or later with NumPy 2.0 or later, SciPy, pandas, matplotlib and openpyxl.
items.title: Parameter identifiability limits in dynamic modelling and control of a brackish-water reverse osmosis system: code and data

items.summary: The manuscript develops a risk-aware operational research framework for strengthening NdFeB permanent-magnet supply-chain resilience under recycling delays, geopolitical disruptions, and uncertain material shortages. It integrates Caputo fractional-order dynamics, delayed recycling flows, strategic procurement and inventory decisions, Pontryagin-type optimality conditions, and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) within a unified decision model. The study makes three principal contributions. First, it formulates a memory-dependent dynamic model and establishes positivity, boundedness, feasible-region, shortage-free equilibrium, and fractional local-stability results. Second, it incorporates procurement, recycling investment, stock accumulation, and stock release as operational controls and derives the corresponding necessary optimality conditions. Third, it introduces a scenario-based CVaR formulation and compares import-dependent, recycling-oriented, stockpiling-based, and integrated resilience policies under a common non-anticipative framework. In the baseline risk-aware analysis, the recycling-oriented and integrated strategies reduce mean shortage by approximately 74% relative to the import-dependent strategy and decrease the empirical CVaR at the 0.95 level of quadratic shortage loss from approximately 0.921 to 0.067.
items.title: A Caputo Fractional-Order Optimal Control Framework for NdFeB Permanent Magnet Supply-Chain Resilience under Recycling Delay and Geopolitical Risk

items.summary: Supplementary research materials accompanying the manuscript “Lifecycle Assurance for AI-Enabled Clinical Software: A Systematic Literature Review." The dataset covers 141 independent studies: 94 primary-practice studies and 47 framework contributions. It documents reported assurance practices, lifecycle coverage, evidence maturity, deployment and operational activities, regulatory engagement, and requirement-to-control-to-evidence mappings. This release includes: • Supplementary_Materials.pdf: review methods, search strings, eligibility rules, coding and appraisal criteria, selection summaries, and reviewer records. • Lifecycle_Assurance_Supplementary_Workbook.xlsx: the final study-level dataset, source rationales, classifications, appraisals, and calculated results. • Replication_Package_v1.0.0.zip: CSV data, Python scripts, reproduction instructions, decision records, and clearly labelled historical versions. Final maturity and regulatory classifications incorporate completed human reconciliation. The reviewer records distinguish the 68-study first-pass comparison from the subsequent 26-study review after exposure to the existing extraction. The scripts reproduce descriptive results, sensitivity analyses, joint-reporting measures, and initial reviewer-agreement statistics. Search-record and source-access limitations are documented in the accompanying materials.

items.summary: Finite-time binding measurements constrain kinetic rates through both a reaction model and its calibration parameters. We characterize the sharp upper bound for the association rate in a three-state conformational-selection model when the dissociation rate, conformational rate, equilibrium constant and concentration scale belong to a prescribed compact joint set. The observations are calibrated bound fractions subject to finitely many closed interval constraints. We first prove that each finite-time bound fraction is strictly increasing in the initial binding-competent population. The physical feasible set at a fixed calibration is therefore an interval in that population. Let V be the calibration parameters with a nonempty physical feasible interval and let C = cl(V) within the joint calibration set. The sharp rate supremum is the reciprocal of the minimum of lambda K0 L / b on C, where L is the lower inverse threshold. Uniform finiteness is equivalent to a positive joint separation from the zero-population limiting curve on C. Explicit examples distinguish pointwise finiteness from uniform finiteness, inaccessible closed boundary points from physical limiting models, and separation by different readings from separation by one fixed reading. A continuous calibration example admits a certified sharp bound. We also state the optical conditions needed to interpret fluorescence as bound population.
items.title: Sharp Identification Bounds for Binding Rates under Joint Calibration Uncertainty

items.summary: Added Animations as GIF : Export GIF... in the animation bar (or Fields > Export Animation as GIF...) saves all frames of the running animation as a looping GIF. Each frame is the view exactly as shown, in its pixel size, and the GIF runs at the speed you see: the bar measures the frames per second actually drawn during playback (shown next to the speed setting, it can be lower than the setting for heavy plots) and the GIF uses that rate. Without a measurement the export first plays the animation for a moment to measure it. All frames share one colour palette, so the colour scale and the field do not change colour from frame to frame. Object groups : Edit > Group (Ctrl+G) puts the selected objects, also solids, sheets and lines together, into one group. A click on a member in the 3D view selects the whole group, so Move, Rotate, Mirror, Copy, Hide or Delete act on all of it; the model tree lists the groups under Groups (rename, ungroup, single members selectable there). Edit > Ungroup (Ctrl+Shift+G) dissolves a group to edit single objects again. Groups are saved in the project. SMD components (C, L, R, Touchstone parts) are inserted as a group of pads, terminations and element sheet, and the integration line of a lumped port or element now moves with its objects. Box selection in the 3D view : a left drag draws a rectangle and selects every object that lies completely inside it (in face, edge or vertex mode: every face, edge or vertex completely inside). Ctrl + drag adds to the selection. A group is selected only when all its members are inside. Hidden objects are skipped; a click still selects one item. Mesh refinement "AURA (EMerge)" , EMerge's own local refinement, with the same error estimate, convergence criterion and curved elements as the other methods. A comparison script measures the time to solution against Local (Delaunay) on the benchmark models ( examples/benchmark/mesher ). Lumped Elements tab : inserts a chip resistor, inductor or capacitor, or a component measured by a Touchstone file: pick the package in the menu of the button and click the position on the board. The part comes with its pads (Perfect E), and its position is the design variables <name>_x/_y/_z, so it moves as a whole. With two traces selected it is placed in the gap between them. Packages 0201, 0402, 0603, 0805, 1206 and the RF series Coilcraft 0402HP/0402HPH/0402CS/0603HP/0603CS and Murata LQW15AN/LQP03TN/GJM03/GJM15 with their body dimensions. Hertzon adds the pads of the land pattern (made like the traces), the element sheet with its Lumped RLC boundary and integration line, and optionally a 3D body with metal terminations (the mounted inductance from the field solution). The ideal value can carry the typical ESL and ESR of the size. Lumped RLC: Model Parallel RLC (as before), Series RLC or Touchstone (.s1p, or .s2p measured in series or as a shunt). The Validation Check reads the Touchstone file; the solver warns when a sweep leaves its frequency range. Draw Integration Line (right click a Lumped Port or Lumped RLC in the project tree): start and end point picked with two clicks in the 3D view, with snapping to vertices and edge centers. Auto Integration Line places it between the conductors again. Changed Field plot animations compute much faster : a phase animation builds the plot (surfaces, cut planes, arrow positions) once and only turns the field for each frame, instead of building the whole plot again. On a patch antenna with 54 000 tetrahedra, 18 frames of Mag_E on the patch take 0.15 s instead of 21 s, on a cut plane 0.2 s instead of 6 s. Phase animation default: 35 steps (was 19) from 0 to 360 deg, for a smoother wave. items.summary: Here we study how mutations which change physical properties of cell proteins (stability) impact population survival and growth. In our model the genotype is presented as a set of N numbers, folding free energies of cells N proteins. Mutations occur upon replications so that stabilities of some proteins in daughter cells differ from those in parent cell by random amounts drawn from experimental distribution of mutational effects on protein stability. The genotype-phenotype relationship posits that unstable proteins confer lethal phenotype to a cell and in addition the cells fitness (duplication rate) is proportional to the concentration of its folded proteins. Simulations reveal that lethal mutagenesis occurs at mutation rates close to 7 mutations per genome per replications for RNA viruses and about half of that for DNA based organisms, in accord with earlier predictions from analytical theory and experiment. This number appears somewhat dependent on the number of genes in the organisms and natural death rate. Further, our model reproduces the distribution of stabilities of natural proteins in excellent agreement with experiment. Our model predicts that species with high mutation rates, tend to have less stable proteins compared to species with low mutation rate.
items.title: Lethal Mutagenesis in Viruses and Bacteria

items.summary: Classical population genetics a priori assigns fitness to alleles without considering molecular or functional properties of proteins that these alleles encode. Here we study population dynamics in a model where fitness can be inferred from physical properties of proteins under a physiological assumption that loss of stability of any protein encoded by an essential gene confers a lethal phenotype. Accumulation of mutations in organisms containing Gamma genes can then be represented as diffusion within the Gamma dimensional hypercube with adsorbing boundaries which are determined, in each dimension, by loss of a protein stability and, at higher stability, by lack of protein sequences. Solving the diffusion equation whose parameters are derived from the data on point mutations in proteins, we determine a universal distribution of protein stabilities, in agreement with existing data. The theory provides a fundamental relation between mutation rate, maximal genome size and thermodynamic response of proteins to point mutations. It establishes a universal speed limit on rate of molecular evolution by predicting that populations go extinct (via lethal mutagenesis) when mutation rate exceeds approximately 6 mutations per essential part of genome per replication for mesophilic organisms and 1 to 2 mutations per genome per replication for thermophilic ones. Further, our results suggest that in absence of error correction, modern RNA viruses and primordial genomes must necessarily be very short. Several RNA viruses function close to the evolutionary speed limit while error correction mechanisms used by DNA viruses and non-mutant strains of bacteria featuring various genome lengths and mutation rates have brought these organisms universally about 1000 fold below the natural speed limit.
items.title: The Hypercube of Life: How Protein Stability Imposes Limits on Organism Complexity and Speed of Molecular Evolution

items.summary: Here we study how mutations which change physical properties of cell proteins (stability) impact population survival and growth. In our model the genotype is presented as a set of N numbers, folding free energies of cells N proteins. Mutations occur upon replications so that stabilities of some proteins in daughter cells differ from those in parent cell by random amounts drawn from experimental distribution of mutational effects on protein stability. The genotype-phenotype relationship posits that unstable proteins confer lethal phenotype to a cell and in addition the cells fitness (duplication rate) is proportional to the concentration of its folded proteins. Simulations reveal that lethal mutagenesis occurs at mutation rates close to 7 mutations per genome per replications for RNA viruses and about half of that for DNA based organisms, in accord with earlier predictions from analytical theory and experiment. This number appears somewhat dependent on the number of genes in the organisms and natural death rate. Further, our model reproduces the distribution of stabilities of natural proteins in excellent agreement with experiment. Our model predicts that species with high mutation rates, tend to have less stable proteins compared to species with low mutation rate.
items.title: Lethal Mutagenesis in Viruses and Bacteria

items.summary: Classical population genetics a priori assigns fitness to alleles without considering molecular or functional properties of proteins that these alleles encode. Here we study population dynamics in a model where fitness can be inferred from physical properties of proteins under a physiological assumption that loss of stability of any protein encoded by an essential gene confers a lethal phenotype. Accumulation of mutations in organisms containing Gamma genes can then be represented as diffusion within the Gamma dimensional hypercube with adsorbing boundaries which are determined, in each dimension, by loss of a protein stability and, at higher stability, by lack of protein sequences. Solving the diffusion equation whose parameters are derived from the data on point mutations in proteins, we determine a universal distribution of protein stabilities, in agreement with existing data. The theory provides a fundamental relation between mutation rate, maximal genome size and thermodynamic response of proteins to point mutations. It establishes a universal speed limit on rate of molecular evolution by predicting that populations go extinct (via lethal mutagenesis) when mutation rate exceeds approximately 6 mutations per essential part of genome per replication for mesophilic organisms and 1 to 2 mutations per genome per replication for thermophilic ones. Further, our results suggest that in absence of error correction, modern RNA viruses and primordial genomes must necessarily be very short. Several RNA viruses function close to the evolutionary speed limit while error correction mechanisms used by DNA viruses and non-mutant strains of bacteria featuring various genome lengths and mutation rates have brought these organisms universally about 1000 fold below the natural speed limit.
items.title: The Hypercube of Life: How Protein Stability Imposes Limits on Organism Complexity and Speed of Molecular Evolution
